catalog_quote: VOKAL PANJANG. Pada akhir kata, kadang-kadang terdapat vokal yang panjang, dan vokal itulah yang ditekankan. Supaya dibacakan dengan benar, dan supaya dibedakan dari kata yang mirip, dalam ejaan bahasa Moma kita menulis vokal panjang dengan dua vokal. Contoh: hamaa, paletaa, toronaa, humpii, woo, mpuu NA'AHI. Vokal panjang tidak terdapat pada awal kata panjang, tetapi dua vokal yang sama kadang-kadang terdapat karena kebetulan bagian terawal dari kata dasar adalah vokal yang sama persis dengan bagian terakhir dari awalan (contoh: na- + ahi, no- + ore). ... Dalam ejaan bahasa Moma, kita tulis koma atas antara dua vokal yang tidak boleh disatukan sebagai satu sukukata. ... LAIPEKUNEMU'I. Bahasa Moma memiliki beberapa enklitik, atau kata tambahan yang menumpang di belakang kata kerja, yang diucapkan sama seperti akhiran tetapi tidak mempengaruhi ucapan kata dasarnya. ... Catatan: Suku kata yang tebal ditekankan. ... Pronunciation notes: Bolded syllables are stressed. ... Me[ha]nitamo [o]lu! ... Na[ra]ha [mpuu]. ... [Ha]ngaku [Ya]na. ... Noba[ngke]letamo? ... para[luu]ku ... Natoro[naa]’adapa. ... [wuu]ku ... po’o[haa]ta ... Hau [hou]. ... Poni[kaa].

new_statements.translation: LONG VOWELS. At the end of a word there is sometimes a long vowel, and it is that vowel which is stressed. So that it is read correctly, and so that it is distinguished from similar words, in Moma spelling we write a long vowel with two vowel letters. Examples: hamaa, paletaa, toronaa, humpii, woo, mpuu

Contoh: hamaa, paletaa, toronaa, humpii, woo, mpuu"); repeated in the 2014 Kelas II reader p. 61 (p. 36) and ALSO in the 2013 teacher guide p. 45 (verification said 'nothing' there; minor). Translation is accurate. WHY I DISAGREE WITH 'unclear': the compilers missed that the SAME open dictionary has a 15-page stress-marked section. Printed pp. 249-263…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Partial statement only: words ending in a (phonemically) long vowel carry stress on that final long vowel, which is why the orthography writes it double to distinguish such words from otherwise similar words. The default position of stress in words without a final long vowel is not stated anywhere in the accessible sources (by implication it is non-final; in closely related Kaili-Pamona languages it is penultimate, but no opened Moma source says so).
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the final-long-vowel case itself; enclitics ('a, 'i, -mo etc.) are said to be pronounced like suffixes 'but do not affect the pronunciation of the base word' (p. xi), which may bear on stress but is not explicit.
new_statements.domain_note: Community trial orthography ('Ejaan Percobaan', agreed 18 June 2008) for the Moma dialect of Kulawi (Bolapapu area, Kec. Kulawi, Kab. Sigi); statement concerns isolated written words.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the Moma dialect (= Kulawi proper / 'North Kulawi', Bolapapu area, Kec. Kulawi, Kab. Sigi), i.e. moma1242 itself. Karsana et al. 2012 use 'bahasa Kulawi' for a cluster of three dialects (Moma = standard, Tomado, Tado); Tado/Lindu is a separate language in Glottolog/ISO (klw), and 'South Kulawi' in older literature refers to Uma (ppk), not Moma.

new_statements.quote: 4. De klemtoon valt in het Koel. op de voorlaatste lettergreep van het stamwoord, hetzij dit primair is of secundair, d.w.z. met een of meer affixen (voor-, in- of achtervoegsels) van een grondwoord afgeleid. Dit wil dus zeggen dat stamwoorden die een of meer der achtervoegsels -i, -a en -ka bevatten, den klemtoon van het grondwoord doen verspringen naar de aan het laatste dier achtervoegsels voorafgaande lettergreep, en dat het achtervoegsel -aka steeds den klemtoon tot zich trekt [...] [p. 9:] Verschillende partikels en interjectioneele voornaamwoorden (zie p. 20 v.) die enclitisch aan het voorafgaande woord worden gehecht hebben op de plaats van den klemtoon geen invloed. Hetzelfde geldt van de bezittelijke voornaamwoorden, die eveneens een enclitisch karakter dragen, dus bónekoe „mijn akker”, béngkana „zijn buffel”, hóoe-kami „ons huis”, enz.
new_statements.translation: 4. In Kulawi the stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the stem word, whether this is primary or secondary, i.e. derived from a root with one or more affixes (prefixes, infixes or suffixes). This means that stem words containing one or more of the suffixes -i, -a and -ka shift the stress of the root to the syllable preceding the last of those suffixes, and that the suffix -aka always attracts the stress [...] [p. 9:] Various particles and interjectional pronouns (see p. 20 ff.) which are attached enclitically to the preceding word have no influence on the place of the stress. The same holds for the possessive pronouns, which also have an enclitic character, thus bónekoe 'my field', béngkana 'his buffalo', hóoe-kami 'our house', etc.
new_statements.citation: Adriani, N. & S. J. Esser. 1939. Koelawische taalstudien. Deel I: Overzicht der spraakkunst, gesprekken en verhalen met vertaling (Bibliotheca Celebica I; also II-III wordlist/texts). Bandoeng: A. C. Nix. viii+91 pp. (Glottolog 107459/591303)

The page scan confirms '-aka' (the Leiden Delpher the scanned textmisreads it as '-aha'; the Utrecht the sc…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's 'fixed: penultimate syllable' reading and as the enclitic-count in the SIL Kamus Saku bold-syllable tally; it is the primary source behind the Himmelmann & Kaufman 2020 sentence and adds the domain statement (stem + suffixes, enclitics excluded) and the long-vowel behaviour that the Kamus Saku 2015 'VOKAL PANJANG' remark records. Found via the KB catalogue: both the Leiden and Utrecht copies are digitized on Delpher (scanned + PDF downloads), though HathiTrust is search-only.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress on the penultimate syllable of the stem word including derivational suffixes (-i, -a, -ka, -aka), so the stress moves rightward when suffixes are added; enclitic particles, interjectional pronouns and possessive pronoun enclitics are outside the stress domain and do not shift it. A long vowel (e.g. -daai, -woerii, roeaa) takes the stress as a whole; when the penultimate vowel can form a diphthong with the preceding vowel the accent falls on the first element, 'as in Ledo' (nampopóida).
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final long vowels/long vowels formed from the antepenult+penult carry the stress as a unit (-daai 'to spoil', roeaa); diphthong-like sequences stress the first element (nampopóida); enclitics excluded from the domain (nangkoni-dako stressed on ngko, nahae-tamo-kowo on ha, moei-radapa on moe). The suffix -aa (doubled -a, p. 23-24 of the same work) always bears stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Adriani & Esser 1939 describe 'Koelawisch' = Kulawi = Moma [myl] (Glottolog language code; Noorduyn 1991 'Kulawi (Moma)'), with occasional comparative notes on Lindu ('Lind.'), Uma ('Oema') and Ledo; the stress statement is about Kulawi proper. Himmelmann & Kaufman 2020 call the language Kulawi and describe it alongside Uma (Pamona-Kaili).

new_statements.quote: A similar pattern can be found in the closely related Kulawi language (Adriani and Esser 1939:9), where prominence is associated with the penultimate syllable of the word including suffixes, but excluding pronominal and adverbial clitics. Enclitics do not attract prominence even when they are disyllabic, as in hóu=kami house=1p.ex.GEN 'our house'. Unlike the Philippine languages discussed above, Kulawi and Uma appear to make a clear distinction between lexical and functional words, with pitch targets anchoring only to lexical words.
new_statements.citation: Himmelmann, Nikolaus P. & Daniel Kaufman. 2020. Austronesia. In Carlos Gussenhoven & Aoju Chen (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of Language Prosody, ch. 28. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Secondary source resting on Adriani & Esser 1939, now opened directly.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prominence on the penultimate syllable of the word including suffixes; pronominal and adverbial enclitics are excluded from the domain and never attract prominence, even when disyllabic. The authors treat this as the same pattern as Uma (Martens 1988), where only lexical words carry pitch accents.
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitics (pronominal, adverbial) do not count; no other exceptions given. Second-hand: the statement is explicitly sourced to Adriani & Esser 1939:9.

Himmelmann & Kaufman 2020 call the language Kulawi and describe it alongside Uma (Pamona-Kaili).
